name: Deuruxolitinib

lead: Deuruxolitinib (Leqselvi) is an oral prescription pill approved in the US for adults with severe alopecia areata, an autoimmune cause of scalp and body hair loss. People with extensive loss follow it for full regrowth.

It blocks JAK enzymes that relay inflammatory signals, which is thought to stop the immune attack on follicles. In the Phase 3 THRIVE-AA1 trial, adults with at least half of their scalp hair lost regrew significantly more hair than on placebo. It is not approved for pattern baldness.

paras: It is a daily pill prescribed and monitored by a doctor, with regrowth building over several months.

The label carries a boxed warning for serious infections, death, cancer, major cardiovascular events and blood clots. Common effects include headache, acne and raised cholesterol. It is contraindicated with certain CYP2C9 conditions and may harm a fetus.

angle.text: Deuruxolitinib is an oral JAK inhibitor approved in the US for severe alopecia areata. By easing the immune attack on follicles it lets scalp and body hair regrow, and trial participants regrew significantly more hair than on placebo.

lead: Deuruxolitinib (brand name Leqselvi; formerly CTP-543) is an oral Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitor approved in the United States for adults with severe alopecia areata, an autoimmune condition that causes patchy to total scalp and body hair loss.[1] It is a deuterated form of a JAK1/JAK2 inhibitor, and in vitro assays reported in the US label showed greater inhibitory potency for JAK1, JAK2 and TYK2 than for JAK3.[1]

Alopecia areata can remove hair from the scalp, eyebrows, lashes and body, and its psychosocial effects are widely described; before JAK inhibitors, treatment of moderate-to-severe disease was historically difficult [2]. Deuruxolitinib received its first global approval in the United States in July 2024 and a UK approval in March 2026 for severe alopecia areata in adults, and is developed by Sun Pharmaceutical Industries [3].

Its efficacy was tested in the Phase 3 THRIVE-AA1 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in adults aged 18 to 65 with at least 50 percent scalp hair loss, which was published in the Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology in 2024.[4] Systematic reviews of JAK inhibitors in alopecia areata describe the class as producing meaningful regrowth while raising safety questions that include infections, acne and laboratory changes.[5][6]

The US label carries a boxed warning covering serious infections, mortality, malignancy, major adverse cardiovascular events and thrombosis.[1] The drug is a prescription medicine for a medical condition; discussion of it in appearance communities is tied mainly to hair regrowth in alopecia areata rather than to pattern hair loss.

paras: The US label lists deuruxolitinib for adults with severe alopecia areata and states it is not recommended in combination with other JAK inhibitors, biologic immunomodulators, cyclosporine or other potent immunosuppressants.[1] It is not indicated for androgenetic (pattern) hair loss.

In the pivotal trials the primary endpoint was the proportion of patients reaching a Severity of Alopecia Tool (SALT) score of 20 or lower, meaning 20 percent or less of the scalp affected, at week 24 [4][7]. In THRIVE-AA1, 29.6 percent on the lower dose and 41.5 percent on the higher dose met it versus 0.8 percent on placebo, and patient-reported satisfaction with hair was 42.1 and 53.0 percent versus 4.7 percent [4]. In THRIVE-AA2, 33.0 and 38.3 percent met it versus 0.8 percent on placebo [7].

THRIVE-AA1 enrolled adults with at least 50 percent scalp hair loss and compared oral deuruxolitinib with placebo; its authors reported significant hair regrowth in the treated groups.[4] Network meta-analyses and systematic reviews comparing JAK inhibitors in moderate-to-severe alopecia areata place deuruxolitinib among the newer agents with positive randomized data.[5][6][8] Reviewers note that most evidence concerns short randomized periods and that relapse after stopping JAK inhibitors has been described across the class.[5][9]

The most common adverse reactions listed on the US label (at least 1 percent) include headache, acne, nasopharyngitis, increased blood creatine phosphokinase and hyperlipidemia.[1] A meta-analysis of placebo-controlled trials of JAK inhibitors in dermatology found an increased risk of acne as an adverse event.[10]

The boxed warning describes increased risk of serious infections including tuberculosis, mortality, malignancy, major adverse cardiovascular events and thrombosis.[1] The label also lists gastrointestinal perforation, lipid elevations, anemia, neutropenia and lymphopenia among warnings, and states that the drug is contraindicated in CYP2C9 poor metabolizers and in people taking moderate or strong CYP2C9 inhibitors.[1] Based on animal studies, the label states it may cause fetal harm.[1] Systematic reviews of JAK inhibitor safety in alopecia areata report mostly mild adverse events in trials but note limited long-term data.[11][12]

JAKs mediate signaling of cytokines and growth factors important to immune function; JAK inhibitors block this signaling, which is thought to interrupt the immune attack on hair follicles in alopecia areata.[1][5] Deuruxolitinib is deuterated, a modification intended to alter its metabolism.[1] Dedicated phase 1 studies examined its pharmacokinetics in renal and hepatic impairment.[13][14]

THRIVE-AA1 (NCT04518995) was a phase 3, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in adults aged 18 to 65 with at least 50 percent scalp hair loss, comparing two deuruxolitinib dose levels with placebo for 24 weeks. Both doses produced significantly higher SALT20 response and satisfaction scores than placebo; most treatment-emergent adverse events were mild or moderate, and the authors noted that longer-term safety and the effect of stopping treatment needed further study [4].

THRIVE-AA2 (NCT04797650) randomized 517 adults aged 18 to 65 with SALT of at least 50 and an episode of at least six months 1:2:1 to the higher dose, lower dose or placebo; the authors report that efficacy and safety support deuruxolitinib as a treatment option, and note that durability was not assessed [7].

A case report describes a man with a 23-year history of alopecia universalis who had not responded to tofacitinib or ritlecitinib and who, after six months of deuruxolitinib, regrew eyebrows and eyelashes while scalp hair stayed largely unchanged.

Phase 1 studies examined pharmacokinetics in renal and hepatic impairment [13][14]. Further registered trials include a phase 3 study in adolescents (NCT07133308, 355 participants, started August 2025) and a phase 3 study in Japanese adults (NCT07617597), both recruiting [15][16]. Review articles summarize the broader JAK inhibitor evidence in alopecia areata [5][6][17][2].

Deuruxolitinib is a newly approved prescription therapy for an autoimmune hair loss condition. In appearance discussions, interest in JAK inhibitors centres on regrowth of scalp, eyebrow and lash hair in alopecia areata; the approved indication does not include pattern (androgenetic) hair loss [1].

timeline.event: Phase 1 studies of renal and hepatic impairment pharmacokinetics begin.[13][14]
First global approval in the USA for severe alopecia areata in adults (July); THRIVE-AA1 results published.[3][4]
UK approval for severe alopecia areata (March).[3]
